targets.title: Die Klassische Dämpfung bei Racine [1928].
targets.evidence_quote: The first and most extensive part of the present study focuses on a computational repetition of Spitzer’s previous, non-digital study.
targets.outcome_computational_quote: Where Spitzer uses a holistic approach, fundamentally a stylistic analysis guided by the guiding principle of the dampening effect, the present study’s method is based on defining formal patterns to be identified in annotated text to identify instances of relevant stylistic patterns.
targets.outcome_robustness_quote: Regarding Racine and the Classical Age, it has become apparent that the stylistic patterns identified by Leo Spitzer, and which in the aggregate produce a dampening effect, again according to Spitzer, are even more frequent in Racine’s work than Spitzer showed. In addition, the analysis was able to show that these patterns are present in varying degrees in Racine’s work and in the work of his contemporaries, but without very strong (or statistically significant) differences, for the most part. The dampening effect, if understood as the aggregate use of individual stylistic patterns, is therefore clearly not an authorial signature style, but the mark of an entire literary genre during a certain period, at the very least.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Alternative operationalization reanalyses the same eleven Racine plays and qualifies the interpretation of a distinctive authorial style. Numerical rerunning was outside the plan because the original was qualitative. The contemporary-author comparison adds texts but the initial reanalysis uses the original works.

reasoning: Same eleven Racine plays constitute the original data, reanalysed digitally with changed annotation and search methods; original edition is unknown, recorded as a boundary uncertainty. Added contemporary plays extend the analysis. German 1931 version of original 1928 essay is the cited target; 1970 French translation is the same work.
